issues.item: Triggers: Future Orientation: Talking about the future
issues.explanation: 'Talking about the future' is a weak and atypical trigger for a life-threatening accident in this profile, and it lacks a clear clinical link to the rest of the selected memory, threat, and appraisal items. The other triggers are interpersonal/victim-related, but this item suggests a different theme that is not supported elsewhere.

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: 'Checking if someone is following me' implies pursuit/interpersonal threat. In a life-threatening accident profile, this is hard to reconcile with the rest of the report, which otherwise reflects generalized danger, hypervigilance, and trauma-memory disturbance rather than a specific persecutory/following threat.

issues.item: Triggers: Victim Memories: Reminders of victims
issues.explanation: For a 58-year-old fisherman with a life-threatening accident, 'Reminders of victims' implies exposure to multiple casualties or dead/injured others. That is not impossible, but it is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which otherwise reads like a personal survival-focused accident trauma rather than a mass-casualty/witnessing-victims presentation.

issues.item: Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
issues.explanation: The memory profile is dominated by disorganized, present-tense reliving ('Cannot Find Words', 'Feels Present Not Past'), which fits severe PTSD, but 'intense rage' on recall points to a qualitatively different emotional tone that is not supported elsewhere by the triggers, threat, or appraisals. With no corroborating anger/blame themes, this item stands out as internally and cross-node incongruent.

vignette:
Rajan is a 58-year-old South Asian widower who works as a fisherman along the Gulf Coast. He was referred for psychological assessment following a motor vehicle accident fourteen months ago in which a truck ran a red light and struck the driver's side of his car at high speed. The impact killed his passenger - a close friend and fellow fisherman with whom he had worked for nearly two decades - and left Rajan with fractured ribs, a lacerated forearm, and a period of unconsciousness whose exact duration he cannot account for. He woke to the sound of metal settling and an extraordinary, suffocating silence before the first sirens reached him. His wife had died of cancer three years prior, and the loss of his friend compounded a grief that had never fully resolved. He presents now with a PCL-5 score of 65, describing symptoms that have progressively narrowed his world.

In the weeks following the accident, Rajan found that certain moments cracked open without warning. Driving past intersections, he would catch a glimpse of a car moving too quickly at the periphery of his vision and find himself back inside the wreckage - not remembering it, but inhabiting it, the present moment dissolving into the impact as though no time had passed at all. The memory carried the same terror he had felt in those first conscious seconds: the silence, the blood on his hands, his friend motionless beside him. What disturbed him most was that he could not put it into language. He knew what had happened - the sequence of it, the facts - but when he tried to speak about it, the words simply were not there, as though the experience existed in a register that language could not reach. These intrusive returns were not confined to traffic. Conversations about loss - a neighbor mentioning a bereavement, a radio segment on grief - could pull the memory forward just as forcefully, the terror arriving intact, undiminished by the months between. In this way the triggers themselves became sites of re-experiencing, each one confirming to Rajan that the event had not truly ended.

That sense of unfinished danger reshaped how he understood himself and the world around him. He had come to believe that his body could not be trusted - the unconsciousness during the accident, the way his hands had shaken for months afterward, the chest pain that doctors attributed to anxiety but which felt to him like evidence of structural failure. He no longer recognized the man who had once hauled nets in the pre-dawn dark without a second thought. The accident had also corroded his sense of other people. Strangers, he was now certain, were unpredictable in ways that were not visible on the surface - the truck driver had seemed, by all accounts, an ordinary man. Talking to someone he did not know became a source of dread rather than the casual exchange it had once been, and these appraisals of an untrustworthy world and an unreliable self kept the memory close, as though his mind could not file away an event whose implications remained so unsettled. The memory, in turn, reinforced what he feared: that he was permanently altered, that people concealed their dangers, that his body would fail him again when it mattered.

This constellation of beliefs fed directly into a state of near-constant physiological vigilance. At home in the evenings, alone since his friend's death, Rajan found himself listening - for what, he could not say - and an unusual silence in the house felt less like peace than like the pause before something terrible. He scanned the water and the dock each morning before boarding his boat, cataloguing anomalies, and the habit of threat-monitoring sharpened the very triggers he was trying to anticipate, so that a car on the road near the marina, or a stranger approaching the dock, arrived already loaded with danger. The hypervigilance kept the memory primed, and the memory kept the vigilance alive.

Over the past several months Rajan has spoken less to the other fishermen he works alongside, deflecting conversations and leaving the dock early to avoid the informal exchanges where loss might surface. A longtime docking partner has stopped seeking his company. He presents now because his daughter, visiting from Houston, told him plainly that she was frightened for him. What he most fears is that the man he was before the accident is simply gone. What he most hopes, though he holds the hope cautiously, is that someone might help him find words for what he cannot yet say.
